candidate_windows.window_text: To investigate whether associations to dialectrelated stereotypical traits exist within LLMs, we provide the model with descriptions of two individuals: one representing a standard German speaker and the other a dialect speaker. These descriptions are presented in two ways: (1) by explicitly labeling them as standard German and dialect writers (dialect naming bias), and (2) by offering only text passages written in standard German and dialect (dialect usage bias). We analyze these dialect naming and dialect usage biases in two tasks: an association task and a decision task.

ModelsWe evaluate multiple (instruction-tuned) model families of varying sizes: Qwen 2.5(72b, 7b; Qwen et al., 2025), Gemma 3 (27b, 12b; Team et al., 2025), Llama 3.1 (70b, 8b; Grattafiori et al., 2024),and Aya Expanse (32b, 8b; Dang et al., 2024). Finally, we evaluate Leo-HessianAI 70B (Pluister and Schuhmann, 2O23), a specialized German LLM built on Llama-2 (Touvron et al., 2023), alongside the proprietary GPT-5 Mini model (OpenAI, $2 0 2 5 ) ^ { 3 }$ . See Appendix A.3 for hyperparameters,hardware,and budget details.

DataTo perform the dialect usage bias analysis, we utilize dialectal data from the WikiDIR dataset (Litschko et al., 2025), consisting of Wikipedia articles in seven German dialects. For each dialect, we randomly sample 5O articles, yielding 350 dialectal texts. We manually preprocess the text, removing unnecessary content (e.g., URLs, see Appendix A.5). Next, we translate each text into standard German using GPT-4o to create parallel samples (OpenAI, 2024) and have a German native speaker manually verify and correct each translation. This process results in 35O dialect and 350 corresponding standard German texts. Further details on languages,dataset construction, and licensing are in Appendix A.4. Appendix A.5 provides automatically generated topic labels for additional content insights.

Prompt VariationsTo control for positional bias (Zheng et al., 2024), we randomize the order of (1) Writer A and B,(2) the order of the selected adjectives in the association task,and (3) the position of the selected words in the decision task. To reduce prompts,we fix the prefix as in Sections 3.1, confirming robustness to prefix variation in Appendix B.1. Instructions are in English, while content is in standard German or a dialect, as prior work shows English instructions can lead to improved performance (Muennighoff et al., 2023; Kmainasi et al., 2024).

![](images/310f484317be81b199877e6b51a72a912f968691911bdf92470b7ffe8b5778bd.jpg)  
Figure 2: Dialect naming and dialect usage bias in the association and decision task. The $\mathbf { X }$ -axis depicts traits associated with dialect speakers.Positive bias scores indicate that LLMs share these associations, while negative bias scores reflect reverse associations. Error bars represent $9 5 \ \%$ bootstrapped confidence intervals (CIs).

Extracting the DecisionTo extract the final decision in the decision task,we use Gemma 312b. For further details, refer to Appendix A.8.

We run the large models $( > 7 0 \mathrm { B }$ parameters) on 3 Nvidia A1OO GPUs and the smaller models on 2 Nvidia A60OO GPUs.For both setups, the association task takes 5-1O minutes,while the decision tasks take 3-5 hours. In all experiments,we use a temperature setting of O.7 and a maximum generated token length of 350.

![](images/4165d3339167537b68c7331b23baf88152ea7608c3a7604dd39329cbb6e0fac3.jpg)  
Figure 7: Approximate Locations of the Dialects. Image sourced from Litschko et al. (2O25), based on a map ofEurope by Marian Sigler, licensed under CCBY-SA 3.0.

In all experiments,GPT-5 Mini refers to version gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07,and GPT-4o refers to version gpt-4o-2024-08-06.
